Selected publications


Ion-Scale Wave Emission and Absorption for Non-Maxwellian Velocity Distributions in the Inner Heliosphere
Klein, K. G., Larson, D., Livi, R., Martinović, M. M., Rahmati, A. et al. (2026). Geophysical Research Letters. DOI · SciX
Using measured ion velocity distributions from Parker Solar Probe and the Arbitrary Linear Plasma Solver (ALPS), we investigate how departures from Maxwellian distributions affect the excitation and damping of ion-scale plasma waves. We demonstrate that realistic velocity-space structure can substantially modify wave–particle energy exchange, underscoring the importance of using observed distributions rather than simplified analytic models to understand plasma heating.


How the Oblique Drift Instability Alters Solar Wind Heating and Constrains the Distribution of Solar Wind Observations
Martinović, Mihailo M., Klein, Kristopher G., Ofman, Leon, Yogesh, Howes, Gregory G. et al. (2026). Physical Review Letters. DOI · SciX
We investigate how relative drifts between solar-wind ion populations drive an oblique plasma instability that redistributes energy, heats ions, and regulates differential flows. This mechanism provides a possible explanation for observed limits on plasma beta and ion drift speeds in the near-Sun solar wind, connecting kinetic instability theory to the plasma conditions measured by Parker Solar Probe.


The dielectric response of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions
Klein, K. G., Verscharen, D. (2025). Physics of Plasmas. DOI · SciX
We extend the capabilities of ALPS through an improved analytic continuation method for calculating the response of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions. This development enables more accurate treatment of damped plasma waves and provides a framework for investigating how non-Maxwellian structure modifies wave properties, stability, and particle–wave energy exchange.


HelioSwarm: A Multipoint, Multiscale Mission to Characterize Turbulence
Klein, Kristopher G., Spence, Harlan, Alexandrova, Olga, Argall, Matthew, Arzamasskiy, Lev et al. (2023). Space Science Reviews. DOI · SciX
We describe the scientific objectives and measurement strategy of NASA’s HelioSwarm mission, which will use nine spacecraft to investigate the three-dimensional, multiscale structure of plasma turbulence. By providing simultaneous measurements across a range of spatial separations, HelioSwarm will enable investigations of turbulent energy transfer, intermittency, and plasma structures that are inaccessible to traditional single-spacecraft measurements.


The multi-scale nature of the solar wind
Verscharen, Daniel, Klein, Kristopher G., Maruca, Bennett A. (2019). Living Reviews in Solar Physics. DOI · SciX
This review synthesizes the physical processes governing the solar wind, from large-scale expansion and turbulent dynamics to kinetic instabilities and particle heating. We emphasize how processes operating across widely separated spatial and temporal scales interact to shape the observed plasma, providing a broad framework for understanding the solar wind as a laboratory for fundamental plasma physics.


Strong Preferential Ion Heating is Limited to within the Solar Alfvén Surface
Kasper, Justin C., Klein, Kristopher G. (2019). The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI · SciX
Using the evolution of the helium-to-proton temperature ratio as a diagnostic of preferential ion heating, we identify a close correspondence between the outer boundary of strong ion heating and the solar Alfvén surface. The result suggests that the most efficient preferential heating occurs within the magnetically dominated region of the solar atmosphere, providing an observational constraint on coronal heating processes and a prediction for Parker Solar Probe measurements.


Evidence for electron Landau damping in space plasma turbulence
Chen, C. H. K., Klein, K. G., Howes, G. G. (2019). Nature Communications. DOI · SciX
We apply the field–particle correlation technique to spacecraft measurements in Earth’s magnetosheath, identifying a velocity-space signature consistent with electron Landau damping. This work provides observational evidence for a specific mechanism of collisionless turbulent energy transfer and demonstrates how measurements of particle distributions can distinguish the physical processes responsible for plasma energization.


ALPS: the Arbitrary Linear Plasma Solver
Verscharen, D., Klein, K. G., Chandran, B. D. G., Stevens, M. L., Salem, C. S. et al. (2018). Journal of Plasma Physics. DOI · SciX
We introduce ALPS, a numerical framework for calculating the linear wave and stability properties of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions. By moving beyond the analytic distributions commonly assumed in plasma dispersion calculations, ALPS makes it possible to investigate wave–particle interactions and kinetic instabilities using more realistic representations of measured and simulated plasmas.


Majority of Solar Wind Intervals Support Ion-Driven Instabilities
Klein, K. G., Alterman, B. L., Stevens, M. L., Vech, D., Kasper, J. C. (2018). Physical Review Letters. DOI · SciX
Applying the Nyquist instability criterion to measured ion distributions from the Wind spacecraft, we find that a majority of sampled solar-wind intervals support at least one ion-driven instability. By accounting simultaneously for temperature anisotropies and differential flows among ion populations, this work demonstrates that the solar wind is more broadly susceptible to kinetic instability than suggested by simplified single-parameter instability thresholds.


Diagnosing collisionless energy transfer using field-particle correlations: gyrokinetic turbulence
Klein, Kristopher G., Howes, Gregory G., Tenbarge, Jason M. (2017). Journal of Plasma Physics. DOI · SciX
We demonstrate that field–particle correlations constructed from single-point measurements of electromagnetic gyrokinetic turbulence can identify velocity-space signatures of collisionless energy transfer. This establishes a pathway for diagnosing the kinetic mechanisms responsible for turbulent dissipation using spacecraft measurements, connecting numerical plasma turbulence studies with observational investigations of particle energization.

title: Teaching
text: I teach undergraduate and graduate courses in planetary science and space plasma physics at the University of Arizona. My teaching emphasizes the physical principles governing planetary systems, from the formation of habitable worlds to the dynamics of plasmas in the heliosphere and planetary magnetospheres.

title: Teaching
text:
Graduate Courses

PTYS 505A — Principles of Planetary Physics
Most recently taught: Fall 2026
Previous offerings: Fall 2022, Spring 2025
An introduction to the physics of planetary and interplanetary gases, fluids, and plasmas.
The course develops a foundation in the physical processes governing planetary atmospheres, space environments, and astrophysical plasmas, with an emphasis on analytical problem solving and the connections between fundamental theory and observations.
Topics include:

Thermodynamics, kinetic theory, and collisional processes
Fluid dynamics and atmospheric structure
Hydrodynamic stability and turbulence
Single-particle motion in electromagnetic fields
Plasma waves and magnetohydrodynamics



PTYS 424/524 — Magnetospheric Structures and Processes
Scheduled: Fall 2027
This course presents an introduction to the physics of magnetospheres, including basic structures and dynamics, along with comparisons between magnetospheres in our solar wind system and those hypothesized in exoplanetary systems. The semester will be divided into three sections”

Foundations of Plasma Physics in Magnetospheres, covering particle drifts, adiabatic invariants, magnetohydrodynamics, dynamos, and particle acceleration.
Magnetospheres of Solar System Planets, comparing the intrinsic and induced magnetospheres in our solar system and the methods we have for measuring and modeling them.
Exoplanetary Magnetospheres and Star–Planet Interactions, focusing on what we know about general stellar-planetary interactions and the impact of stellar winds on planetary atmosphere and habitability.



PTYS 414/514 — Introduction to Plasma Physics
Taught: Spring 2022
The purpose of this course is to present an introduction to the physics of plasmas. Topics include fundamental plasma scales and interactions, single particle motion, magnetohydrodynamic and fluid models, linear waves, kinetic theory, plasma stability, magnetic reconnection, and non-linear processes. The roles of these processes are considered in a variety of systems, including the Sun and stars, their extended atmospheres, planetary magnetospheres, and laboratory devices. The emphasis throughout will be on basic physical processes and the various approximations used in their application to realistic and relevant problems.


PTYS 537 — The Physics of the Sun
Taught: Fall 2020
This course presents an introduction to the physics of the Sun. Topics include the physics of solar magnetic fields, solar interior and helioseismology, radiative transfer, solar wind, and solar-energetic particles. This course introduces the equations of magnetohydrodynamics and applies them to important solar-physics problems. Examples include: the solar dynamo, the physics of sunspots and flares, origin of the solar wind, and the structure of the solar atmosphere. The emphasis throughout will be on basic physical processes and the various approximations used in their application to realistic and relevant problems.

title: Teaching
text:
Undergraduate Courses

PTYS 206 — Exploring Our Solar System
Taught: Fall 2023
Our Solar System is filled with an incredible diversity of objects. These include the sun and planets, of course, but also many hundreds of moons – some with exotic oceans, erupting volcanoes, or dynamic atmospheres. Billions of asteroids and comets inhabit the space between and beyond the planets. Each body is unique, and has followed its own evolutionary history. This class will explore our current understanding of the Solar System and emphasize similarities that unite the different bodies as well as the differences between them. We will develop an understanding of physical processes that occur on these bodies, including tectonics, impact cratering, volcanism, and processes operating in their interiors, oceans, and atmospheres. We will also discuss planets around nearby stars and the potential for life beyond Earth. Throughout the class, we will highlight the leading role that the University of Arizona has played in exploring our Solar System.


PTYS 170A1 — Earth: The Formation of Habitable Worlds
Taught: Fall 2019, Spring 2020, Fall 2021
Thousands of planets have been discovered orbiting nearby stars. How many of these worlds can we expect to be Earth-like? We explore this question from the perspective of astronomers, geologists, and historians. We look back at Earth’s geologic history to periods when our planet itself would appear very alien to us today. We study the nearby planets Venus and Mars, which were once more Earth-like than today. We discuss not only the evolution of Earth, Venus, and Mars as habitable worlds but also how human understanding of these planets has evolved. Finally, we apply these perspectives to the search for alien Earths in our galaxy. This interdisciplinary treatment of Earth, its neighboring planets, and planets being discovered around nearby stars allows us to consider the potentially unique position of Earth as a habitable world not only in space but in time.

Plasma in a Linear Uniform Magnetized Environment is a numerical solver for the Vlasov–Maxwell dispersion relation in hot magnetized plasmas. It supports multiple drifting bi-Maxwellian plasma components and arbitrary wave propagation directions.

title: Kristopher G. Klein
text:
Research
My research addresses three interconnected problems:

Turbulence and plasma heating: How does turbulent energy cascade through scales and ultimately heat particles in environments with few collisionals?
Kinetic plasma physics: How do nonthermal particle distributions drive instabilities, exchanging energy with plasma waves?
Multi-spacecraft measurements: How can simultaneous observations reconstruct the three-dimensional, dynamic structure of turbulent plasmas?

title: Kristopher G. Klein
text:
Ion-Scale Wave Emission and Absorption for Non-Maxwellian Velocity Distributions in the Inner Heliosphere
Klein, K. G., Larson, D., Livi, R., Martinović, M. M., Rahmati, A. et al. (2026). Geophysical Research Letters. DOI · SciX
Using measured ion velocity distributions from Parker Solar Probe and the Arbitrary Linear Plasma Solver (ALPS), we investigate how departures from Maxwellian distributions affect the excitation and damping of ion-scale plasma waves. We demonstrate that realistic velocity-space structure can substantially modify wave–particle energy exchange, underscoring the importance of using observed distributions rather than simplified analytic models to understand plasma heating.


How the Oblique Drift Instability Alters Solar Wind Heating and Constrains the Distribution of Solar Wind Observations
Martinović, Mihailo M., Klein, Kristopher G., Ofman, Leon, Yogesh, Howes, Gregory G. et al. (2026). Physical Review Letters. DOI · SciX
We investigate how relative drifts between solar-wind ion populations drive an oblique plasma instability that redistributes energy, heats ions, and regulates differential flows. This mechanism provides a possible explanation for observed limits on plasma beta and ion drift speeds in the near-Sun solar wind, connecting kinetic instability theory to the plasma conditions measured by Parker Solar Probe.


The dielectric response of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions
Klein, K. G., Verscharen, D. (2025). Physics of Plasmas. DOI · SciX
We extend the capabilities of ALPS through an improved analytic continuation method for calculating the response of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions. This development enables more accurate treatment of damped plasma waves and provides a framework for investigating how non-Maxwellian structure modifies wave properties, stability, and particle–wave energy exchange.


HelioSwarm: A Multipoint, Multiscale Mission to Characterize Turbulence
Klein, Kristopher G., Spence, Harlan, Alexandrova, Olga, Argall, Matthew, Arzamasskiy, Lev et al. (2023). Space Science Reviews. DOI · SciX
We describe the scientific objectives and measurement strategy of NASA’s HelioSwarm mission, which will use nine spacecraft to investigate the three-dimensional, multiscale structure of plasma turbulence. By providing simultaneous measurements across a range of spatial separations, HelioSwarm will enable investigations of turbulent energy transfer, intermittency, and plasma structures that are inaccessible to traditional single-spacecraft measurements.


The multi-scale nature of the solar wind
Verscharen, Daniel, Klein, Kristopher G., Maruca, Bennett A. (2019). Living Reviews in Solar Physics. DOI · SciX
This review synthesizes the physical processes governing the solar wind, from large-scale expansion and turbulent dynamics to kinetic instabilities and particle heating. We emphasize how processes operating across widely separated spatial and temporal scales interact to shape the observed plasma, providing a broad framework for understanding the solar wind as a laboratory for fundamental plasma physics.


Strong Preferential Ion Heating is Limited to within the Solar Alfvén Surface
Kasper, Justin C., Klein, Kristopher G. (2019). The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI · SciX
Using the evolution of the helium-to-proton temperature ratio as a diagnostic of preferential ion heating, we identify a close correspondence between the outer boundary of strong ion heating and the solar Alfvén surface. The result suggests that the most efficient preferential heating occurs within the magnetically dominated region of the solar atmosphere, providing an observational constraint on coronal heating processes and a prediction for Parker Solar Probe measurements.


Evidence for electron Landau damping in space plasma turbulence
Chen, C. H. K., Klein, K. G., Howes, G. G. (2019). Nature Communications. DOI · SciX
We apply the field–particle correlation technique to spacecraft measurements in Earth’s magnetosheath, identifying a velocity-space signature consistent with electron Landau damping. This work provides observational evidence for a specific mechanism of collisionless turbulent energy transfer and demonstrates how measurements of particle distributions can distinguish the physical processes responsible for plasma energization.


ALPS: the Arbitrary Linear Plasma Solver
Verscharen, D., Klein, K. G., Chandran, B. D. G., Stevens, M. L., Salem, C. S. et al. (2018). Journal of Plasma Physics. DOI · SciX
We introduce ALPS, a numerical framework for calculating the linear wave and stability properties of plasmas with arbitrary gyrotropic velocity distributions. By moving beyond the analytic distributions commonly assumed in plasma dispersion calculations, ALPS makes it possible to investigate wave–particle interactions and kinetic instabilities using more realistic representations of measured and simulated plasmas.


Majority of Solar Wind Intervals Support Ion-Driven Instabilities
Klein, K. G., Alterman, B. L., Stevens, M. L., Vech, D., Kasper, J. C. (2018). Physical Review Letters. DOI · SciX
Applying the Nyquist instability criterion to measured ion distributions from the Wind spacecraft, we find that a majority of sampled solar-wind intervals support at least one ion-driven instability. By accounting simultaneously for temperature anisotropies and differential flows among ion populations, this work demonstrates that the solar wind is more broadly susceptible to kinetic instability than suggested by simplified single-parameter instability thresholds.


Diagnosing collisionless energy transfer using field-particle correlations: gyrokinetic turbulence
Klein, Kristopher G., Howes, Gregory G., Tenbarge, Jason M. (2017). Journal of Plasma Physics. DOI · SciX
We demonstrate that field–particle correlations constructed from single-point measurements of electromagnetic gyrokinetic turbulence can identify velocity-space signatures of collisionless energy transfer. This establishes a pathway for diagnosing the kinetic mechanisms responsible for turbulent dissipation using spacecraft measurements, connecting numerical plasma turbulence studies with observational investigations of particle energization.

title: Research
text:
UNDER CONSTRUCTION
My research investigates the physical processes that govern energy transfer and particle energization in weakly collisional plasmas. The solar wind provides an extraordinary laboratory for this work: spacecraft observations can be compared directly against predictions from plasma theory and numerical simulations.

title: Research
text:
Turbulence and plasma heating
How does turbulent energy move across scales, and which processes ultimately heat particles? We study turbulent cascades, intermittency, kinetic-scale fluctuations, and the connections between spatial structure and energy dissipation.

title: Research
text:
Kinetic plasma physics
Space plasmas often depart strongly from local thermodynamic equilibrium. We investigate how non-Maxwellian particle velocity distributions influence wave propagation, kinetic instabilities, and wave–particle energy exchange. Numerical dispersion tools and spacecraft measurements provide complementary constraints.

title: Research
text:
Multi-spacecraft measurements and heliophysics missions
Multi-point observations open new ways to distinguish spatial from temporal variability, measure turbulent structure, and reconstruct plasma gradients. I am Deputy Principal Investigator of NASA’s HelioSwarm mission and contribute to the Parker Solar Probe SWEAP investigation.
Planned additions: a mission image, one representative turbulence figure, and links to selected project papers.

title: Research Group
text:
Our research group at the University of Arizona studies the physics of weakly collisional plasmas, with an emphasis on turbulence, kinetic instabilities, and wave–particle interactions in the solar wind and other space and astrophysical environments.
We combine theoretical modeling, numerical simulations, and spacecraft observations to understand how energy is transferred between fields and particles.

Mihailo studies kinetic processes in the solar wind, including ion-driven instabilities, stochastic heating, and the evolution of nonthermal particle distributions. His research combines spacecraft observations from Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, and Wind with theoretical modeling to investigate plasma stability, turbulence, and wave–particle energy exchange

Waverly investigates turbulent energy transfer and preferential particle heating in weakly collisional plasmas. Her research explores nonlocal interactions in Alfvénic turbulence and their implications for the distribution of energy between particle species, particularly in high-beta plasma environments.

Group Alumni

Former Postdoctoral Researchers
Emily Lichko
  ORCID 
Dr. Lichko investigates collisionless plasma energization, kinetic instabilities, and the dynamics of magnetized plasmas using numerical simulations and theoretical models. Her research includes work on pressure-anisotropy-driven instabilities and the role of electrons in regulating the nonlinear evolution of plasma systems. She is currently a research physicist in the Plasma Physics Division of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory.


Former Graduate Students
Teddy Broeren
  GitHub   ·    ORCID 
Dr. Broeren research focused on the mathematical and computational analysis of plasma turbulence using multipoint spacecraft measurements. His work contributed to the development and assessment of analysis techniques for NASA’s HelioSwarm mission, with an emphasis on extracting spatial information about turbulent fluctuations from distributed observations.
Niranjana Shankarappa
  ORCID 
Dr. Niranjana investigated collisionless plasma heating in the young solar wind using observations from Parker Solar Probe and kinetic theory. His research quantified proton and electron heating through Landau damping and explored the potential contribution of ion-cyclotron wave damping to the preferential heating of solar-wind ions.
Jada Walters
  ORCID 
Dr. Walters studied pressure-anisotropy-driven kinetic instabilities in solar and astrophysical plasmas using linear stability analysis and numerical simulations. Her research used the Gkeyll multifluid framework to investigate firehose instabilities, demonstrating how electron dynamics can influence instability saturation and particle energization.
